_comment: Autarkia's appearance vocabulary. Anima ships the machinery that reads this; everything here
is content. Edit it with tools/appearance-preview (scripts/appearance-preview.sh), which reads
this exact file and runs the exact compositor the game runs.
Ramp shades are fixed point: [hue tenths of a degree, saturation thousandths, value thousandths],
deepest shade first. A ramp replaces one authored colour per shade, and it is written one of two
ways. A bare ARRAY of shades means the art is drawn in the reserved index colours FF0000, FF0001,
FF0002, ... (see Shades) — the right default for art authored from scratch. An OBJECT may add
'keys': the real colours the art is actually drawn in, one per shade, deepest first. That is what
lets a layer be painted in visible colour and still recolour per agent, and it is why 'beard' is
spelled that way — its art is drawn in real browns rather than in index colours.
Either way, a pixel that is neither transparent nor one of that ramp's keys is left exactly as
authored, on purpose, so a stray colour stays visible instead of quietly becoming a shade nobody
chose. Keys must be distinct, and a ramp's keys are part of what its NAME means — two ramps with
the same name and different keys would collide in the bake cache.
A slot marked 'optional' is allowed to draw nothing — a beard, blood, grime. Without it the
editor would rightly complain that a selector with no '*' rule leaves the slot empty for some
combination of parameters, which for these slots is the entire point.
A slot whose selector reads a parameter that changes many times a second MUST be 'dynamic',
or every change re-bakes the shared static base that the whole split exists to protect. The
beard reads 'speaking', so it is dynamic even though a beard itself does not come and go.
Everyone is dressed: 'shirt' and 'trousers' have a wildcard and always draw, in two separate
cloth ladders, because one colour for both is what makes a crowd read as a uniform rather than
as people. 'uniform' is the job layer over the top — optional, one rule per job, and only
'farmer' exists so far. Adding a job is one rule and one PNG.
A texture may name a FAMILY rather than a file: 'autarkia:person/{gender}/hair/{hairstyle}'
means every PNG in that folder is a hairstyle. Nothing lists them — the folder IS the list, so
drawing a new one makes it choosable with no edit here. In game the parameter comes from the
person; in the editor it is a dropdown of what exists.
ART IS SPLIT BY GENDER, and the split is a path and nothing more: male/ and female/ each hold
their own body, hair, shirts, pants and beard, while the face (eyes, mouth) and the job layer
(uniforms) are shared because they are drawn the same on anybody. Two things follow, and both
fall out of the paths rather than out of any rule written anywhere:
- A ROLL only ever offers what exists for that person. 'what shirts are there' has two
answers once the art is split, and a settler is rolled against the narrower one — handing a
man a shirt drawn only for a woman would resolve to a path with no file behind it, and that
failure is not an error, it is a torso that draws nothing for the life of the world.
- A family a gender has NO folder for is simply not offered to them. That is the whole reason
only men have beards: there is no female/beard, so there is nothing to roll, and no code
anywhere says anything about who may have one.
Every file in a family shares the slot's ONE recolouring rule. If that rule is a ramp, every
member must be drawn in the same palette — a ramp cannot have two identity colours. A family
whose members come from different sources therefore uses 'retint' instead, which measures its
reference per file: that is why 'hair' is drawn that way, and why 'shirt' became so once a
green blouse joined a teal shirt. The cost is real and worth knowing: a ramp gives per-shade
control and a retint moves every pixel by one HSV difference, so a family that IS one palette
is still better served by a ramp.
The body is a family too: 'autarkia:person/{gender}/body/{model}' picks slim.png or wide.png,
and the editor draws the slim arm model for 'slim' — the geometry IS the parameter the skin
is chosen by, so there is one control and not two. Both bodies share the slot's ramp, so both
must be drawn in the same palette — they are, exactly, which is what makes one ramp enough.
Vanilla armour renders OVER the whole baked skin, so cloth only ever shows where armour is not.
A RAMP MUST DESCRIBE ITS ART. Its keys are the exact colours the file is drawn in and there is
one shade per key, so redrawing a layer with a different palette means recalibrating its ramp —
otherwise the lookup misses every pixel and the layer simply stops responding to its binding,
silently and completely. The editor's problems list counts the pixels a ramp does not know.
A ramp is for art drawn as a SHADE MAP — a handful of flat tones. Art that is a painting uses
'retint' instead: it measures the HSV difference between one reference colour in the file and
the target, and applies that one difference to every pixel, so a hundred and thirty hand-mixed
skin tones keep their relationships and move together. The body is drawn that way.
Each garment has its own ramp because each is drawn in its own palette. 'trousers' carries the
shoes as well: their keys are greys, and saturation is a RATIO, so a zero-saturation key gives a
zero-saturation shade whatever CLOTH_B becomes — the shoes stay grey and only track its
lightness. Nothing special was needed for that; it falls out of the arithmetic.
Slot order is composite order, so 'trousers' is declared before 'shirt' and the shirt hangs
over the waistband rather than being tucked into it.
A rule's 'texture' may be a LIST, best first. Layers that reach the arms need it: narrowing an
arm moves its faces on the sheet, so a sleeve drawn for wide arms lands on the wrong pixels of
a slim one. Listing ['x_{model}', 'x'] says draw the specific file if somebody made one and the
shared file otherwise — which is the rule an artist works to. Two selector rules cannot say it:
a rule matches on PARAMETERS, so a slim rule would match whether or not the art exists and the
layer would vanish instead of falling back.
'retint' with no 'from' measures its reference from the ART — each texture's own most common
opaque colour. That is what lets one slot wear files drawn from different sources: short hair
off Steve is a dark brown and long hair off Alex is a light ginger, and no single list of ramp
keys can serve both. With a measured reference nothing needs standardising and nothing needs
recalibrating when a file is redrawn.
Everything a person is made of lives under textures/person: male/ and female/ hold one
folder per CHOICE (body, hair, shirts, pants, beard), and eyes/, mouth/ and uniforms/ are
shared. A folder is a family and its files are the options, so adding a shirt is dropping a
PNG into that gender's shirts/ — the picker lists it, and nothing here changes.
A LADDER is the set of values a colour binding may take, in order, and a genotype stores the
POSITION rather than the colour — which is what makes a tone heritable and what stops a crowd
being a scatter of unrelated RGB. Written as a bare array it is drawn triangularly: common in
the middle of the list, rare at the ends. Written as an object it carries 'weights', one per
colour, any scale, relative to each other — which replaces an accident of ordering with a
statement, so moving a colour up the list no longer changes how often it appears.
The weights here are meant to be argued with. They say: brown hair and brown eyes carry a
settlement while red and blond are the ones you notice; cloth is undyed cream and tan before
anybody pays for colour, earth dyes are cheap, and purple is worth remarking on; work trousers
are brown and grey because that is not where dye gets spent. None of that is a fact about the
world, it is a look, and it is one number away from being a different one.
A weight of ZERO excludes a colour without removing it, and that matters more than it reads: a
genotype stores a position, so DELETING an entry renumbers every colour after it and silently
repaints every settler already carrying a later one. Switch a colour off; do not delete it.
Family members (hairstyles, shirts) are NOT weighted and are drawn uniformly. A colour ladder is
a spectrum, so 'commoner in the middle' means something about a population; a hairstyle has no
middle for a bias to be about. A rare hat would want odds stated per member, not inferred from
where its file happens to sort.
A STATE is a suffix that falls back, exactly as a model cut is: eyes/{mood}_blink before
eyes/{mood}, mouth/{mood}_open before mouth/{mood}, beard/{beard}_speaking before
beard/{beard}. So a blink is drawn once per expression that needs its own, and every
expression without one simply does not blink. Draw happy_blink and
a happy face blinks; until then it holds its happy eyes through the blink, which is a gap you
can see rather than a wrong pixel. Listing a third candidate — {mood}_blink, neutral_blink,
{mood} — would make every expression borrow a generic blink instead; one line, if that reads
better than not blinking.
Suffixed files are never offered in a picker. A blink is not an expression and a slim cut is
not a hairstyle — both are another way of drawing a choice somebody already made.
